Capital One. What's in your wallet? Terms apply. Details at CapitalOne.com.
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Culver City, California, I'm Dua Halisa Kautau.
High king tides, the exceptionally high tides that just hit the San Francisco and San Diego
coastline, are apparently over from now. In the East, heavy rains and high winds postponed the
100th annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade to Saturday. From his Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm
Beach, President Trump signed a major disaster declaration for the state of Florida following
a record 17 inches of rain. It's been raining continuously. It's the craziest thing. It's stopped
now. Very unusual for Florida, but it's record-setting rains in a lot of areas in Florida where
we're beating up pretty badly and we're releasing funding, immediate funding.
Trump also approved funding for debris removal and emergency protective measures in connection
with Hurricane Isaias, totaling an estimated $100 million. The Kremlin is dismissing independent
media investigations that claim Russia's battlefield losses in Ukraine run as high as
700,000 soldiers. In Paris Charles-Maine's reports, the findings are based on data allegedly stolen
from Russian government servers. The data was obtained by Ukrainian and Belarusian hacker groups
that claimed to have infiltrated Russia's state statistics agency and then distributed what they
stole to a handful of Russian independent news outlets operating in exile. Their subsequent
research found Russia registered nearly half a million military deaths by September 2026.
However, several outlets projected the real number was much higher, over 700,000,
once delays in entering data and soldiers missing but presumed dead were factored in.
The Kremlin spokesman urged the public to ignore the findings,
saying only Russia's defense ministry could be trusted with information on war losses.
Yet that ministry last announced casualty figures in September of 2022, when it said nearly 6,000
troops had been killed in battle. Charles-Maine's NPR News, Moscow. Research in the journal science
offers a potential new approach to treating female infertility. NPR's Ping Huang reports
it aims to improve the quality of aging eggs. For most women, fertility declines in middle age.
Eggs, held in reserve for a lifetime, start developing chromosomal abnormalities.
Now, researchers at the Max Planck Institute have developed a way to hold those chromosomes together
so they're less likely to separate improperly. The lab-based approach glues pairs of chromosomes
together inside the egg and then releases them at the right time during cell division.
In eggs from old mice, the approach reduced the rate of premature chromosomal separation so much
that the rates were in line with those in young mice. The approach seems to work as intended in
donated human eggs, too, at least in early experiments. More research is needed to see
whether this approach improves the chances that those aged eggs will result in healthy babies.
Ping Huang, NPR News. This is NPR.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky says Russia is preparing a new mass attack on his country's
energy infrastructure in the coming days. He announced this in his latest video address,
warning the public to pay close attention to air alarms of missile threats.
Areas that have previously been hit hard include the Nipro, Harkiv and Odessa regions.
Ukraine asked the U.S. to accelerate its deliveries of air defense missiles,
but Washington has not yet said when this would happen.
It is no surprise that American families traditionally avoid talking politics when
gathering at the dinner table for the Thanksgiving holiday, and Piers-Alina Moore reports on a new
poll from Marist University that finds a majority of Americans tend to steer clear of the subject
when they visit with friends and family. In a national survey of adults planning
to celebrate the holiday, nearly six in 10 say they dread the thought of discussing politics
at the Thanksgiving dinner table this year. It's an increase from four years earlier,
when 42 percent said they felt that way. So a desire to avoid the topic may have gone up,
but many still admit it's hard to avoid. Six in 10 also said they still think it's
very likely or somewhat likely the topic comes up. Alina Moore, NPR News.
Wall Street is on a holiday break today. Stocks will resume tomorrow but close at 1 p.m. Eastern.
A.I. stocks lost momentum yesterday, losing ground for a second day
after Monday's record rally on the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia's CEO.
I'm Dua Lisa Kautau, NPR News in Culver City.
This message comes from the National Audubon Society. Want to protect the planet? For Audubon,
it all begins with birds. Their work protecting birds and habitats for over a century has helped
bring back species like the bald eagle. Now they need you to tackle the threats birds face today,
because when birds thrive, so does the planet. Become a member by December 31st
to get the spring issue of their quarterly magazine. Give today at audubon.org/npr.

topics.text: Trump signs Florida disaster declaration after record 17 inches of rain, approves Isaias funding
Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade postponed to Saturday due to heavy rain and high winds
King tides over for now after hitting San Francisco and San Diego coastlines
Kremlin dismisses independent media claims that Russian battlefield losses reached 700,000 soldiers
Max Planck researchers develop chromosome-gluing method that may improve aging egg quality
Zelensky warns Russia preparing new mass attack on Ukraine's energy infrastructure
Marist poll finds most Americans dread discussing politics at Thanksgiving dinner this year
Wall Street takes holiday break; AI stocks lost momentum after Nvidia's Jensen Huang reinstatement
